events.text: For three hundred years your forefoot has had three claws, and you never missed the fourth. Then one spring morning the skin between them splits, and a fourth claw comes out wet and pale and curved like a new moon. You close the foot. For the first time in your life it closes all the way, the way a hand closes around something it means to keep.

choices.text: Close it again and again, until it is yours

effects.log: You spend a whole season closing your foot on nothing. Fish learn to stay out of that corner of the pool. By autumn the claw is black and hard as temple bronze.

choices.text: Hold up the empty foot to the sky

effects.log: A woodcutter on the ridge sees a serpent the length of a barge holding up one empty claw to the clouds, as if asking for something. He tells it in the market for the rest of his life.

choices.text: Touch the bottom of the pool with it, gently

effects.log: You pick up a single river pebble without scratching it. A claw that can hold a pebble can hold a pearl. You put the pebble back exactly where it was.

events.text: The four-clawed foot changes how the humans speak of you. Old men on the bank count the claws in the mist and go quiet. Four claws is what the old paintings give the dragons of kings. A village elder comes down to the water with a brush and a scroll and asks, very politely, if you would hold still.

choices.text: Hold still for the painting

effects.log: The painting hangs in the village shrine for two hundred years. The claws are a little too large. You decide you like it that way.

choices.text: Put the claw in the water, out of sight

effects.log: The elder paints you with three claws, out of politeness. Some things are not for villages to know yet.

choices.text: Rake the claw across the rock so they never forget

effects.log: Four grooves in the black rock, each as deep as a forearm. The children dare each other to lie in them. Nobody throws a stone into the pool again.

events.text: A failed swordsman has been meditating on the rock at the edge of your lake for three winters. Nobody comes to fetch {him}. {He} eats pine needles and lake water and talks to the mist about a sword art that never worked. You have a thousand years of breathing in you: the way water moves, the way qi coils. Nobody has ever written it down. You could.

choices.text: Rise from the water and speak the whole record to {him}

mem.note: gave me the record of the abyss

effects.log: It takes nine nights. You speak; {npc} writes on the inside of {his} robe, then on bark, then on the rock itself. At dawn on the tenth day {he} stands up and moves like water. {He} weeps without seeming to notice.

choices.text: Give {him} one line only, and see what {he} does with it

effects.log: "Do not fight the current. Be the current." {npc} sits with it for another year. Then {he} cuts a falling leaf in half without touching it, and laughs like a child.

choices.text: Leave {him} to the mist; heaven teaches who it chooses

effects.log: In spring the rock is empty. You hear later that {npc} became a ferryman downriver, and was happy, which is also a kind of enlightenment.

events.text: {npc} has built a hall of pine logs on your shore and taken eleven disciples, mostly orphans and failures like {he} was. {He} has named it the Coiled Lake Sect. On the day of the founding {he} kneels at the water with a bowl of clear rice liquor and asks you to bless the gate.

choices.text: Bless it: rain on the roof, a rainbow over the gate

effects.log: A soft rain falls on the new hall and nowhere else. The eleven disciples will tell it to their own disciples. The Coiled Lake Sect is born under your rain.

choices.text: Bless it, with one law: no one of this gate ever hunts a beast for its core

effects.log: {npc} carves the law over the gate before the sign with the sect name. The first rule of the Coiled Lake Sect is a rule about you.

choices.text: Refuse. You gave a record, not a name

effects.log: {npc} bows and builds it anyway, quietly. The sect never uses your name, which makes the villages say it louder.

events.text: {npc} is old. {He} is carried down to the shore on a litter by four disciples who are older now than {he} was when {he} first sat on the rock. {He} wants to say goodbye to the water.

choices.text: Lay your head on the shore beside the litter

effects.log: An old human hand on scales the size of roof tiles. "I was nothing," {npc} says. "You made me a beginning." {He} dies at the turn of the year, and the whole sect wears white to the lake.

choices.text: Give {him} the last breath of the record: the part you kept back

effects.log: {npc} listens with closed eyes, nods once, and says: "Ah. So that was it." Then {he} smiles and does not open {his} eyes again. The last line goes into the grave with {him}, and the sect searches for it for three hundred years.

choices.text: Stay deep. You do not do farewells

effects.log: The disciples wait until dark and carry {npc} home. That night the lake is so still the stars lie on it unbroken. Some of them say that was your farewell.

events.text: A hundred years on, the Coiled Lake Sect has four hundred disciples and stone halls where the pine hall was. Its patriarch wears a robe embroidered with a four-clawed serpent. You hear, from the gossip of fishermen, that the sect has started collecting a rain tax from the valley. In your name.

choices.text: Rise at their great ceremony and say, in front of everyone, that you take no tax

effects.log: Four hundred disciples on their faces in the mud. The patriarch never collects another coin. The valley sends you rice cakes for the rest of the century, which you did not ask for either.

choices.text: Let it go. Humans need something to argue about

effects.log: The tax goes on. The valley learns to fear the lake a little, the way you fear a lord you have never seen.

choices.text: Dry the sect's wells for one summer

effects.log: Every well inside the sect walls goes dry while the valley wells overflow. The patriarch takes the message, and the coins back to the farmers, by the end of the month.

events.text: The Coiled Lake Sect is at war. A demonic sect has come over the pass with three hundred blades, and the disciples have barred the gate and lit the signal fires. The youngest of them, a girl of ten with a wooden sword, has run down to the water and is shouting your name into it.

choices.text: Come up out of the lake and end it

ok.log: A wave the height of the gate comes out of a lake with no wind on it. The demonic sect does not reach the second wall. The girl with the wooden sword becomes the sect's ninth patriarch, and every one of her disciples learns your name first.

fail.log: Their elder has a halberd that bites scale. You drive them off, but you carry the wound into the deep for a decade. (-25 health)

choices.text: Send fog over the pass so the sect can choose its own fight

effects.log: Fog so thick the demonic sect fights itself on the pass. The Coiled Lake Sect wins its war mostly on its own, and is the better for it.

choices.text: Stay down. A sect that cannot hold its gate should not have a gate

effects.log: They hold, barely. The girl with the wooden sword never forgives the lake. When she is old she tells her disciples that gods are not to be relied upon, and she is not wrong.

events.text: In the sect's library there is now a shelf of commentaries on the record you spoke to a ragged swordsman long ago. They argue over every word. A scholar-disciple rows out to the middle of the lake and asks the water, very respectfully, what the third line actually means.

choices.text: Tell the truth: you said it the way water says things, it means what it does

effects.log: The scholar rows back and writes the four-hundredth commentary, which is the first one to be right. Nobody believes it.

choices.text: Give the sect a new line for a new age

effects.log: One new line, spoken to the mist. The sect calls it the Second Record and builds a pavilion just to keep it in.

choices.text: Splash the boat and let them keep arguing

effects.log: A sect needs something to argue over in winter. You have given them centuries of it.

events.text: A youth comes to the lake with a sword too fine for {his} clothes and a face that has already learned how to lie. {He} is the most gifted human you have seen in four hundred years. {He} kneels in the shallows, cold to the waist, for nine days, and asks to be taught.

choices.text: Teach {him}. Gifts like that should not be wasted

effects.log: {He} learns in a month what took the swordsman on the rock a year. {He} never once asks what the arts are for.

choices.text: Teach {him} only the half that heals

effects.log: {npc} learns it all and asks for the rest. You say no. {He} bows exactly as deep as courtesy requires and not one hair deeper.

choices.text: Send {him} away. Something in those eyes

effects.log: {npc} stands up out of the water, dripping, and looks at you for a long time. Then {he} goes. You find out years later what {he} became, and you are glad it was not with your arts.

events.text: News comes up the river with the fishing boats: a swordsman who fights like a flood has drowned a whole rival clan in their own courtyard by pulling the well up through the floor. The murim calls {him} the Drowning Blade. You know the breathing behind that technique. It is yours. It is {npc}.

choices.text: Call {him} home with a storm

effects.log: Three days of storm over the lake and nowhere else. On the fourth day a figure in black comes down the mountain path, sword at {his} hip, smiling.

choices.text: Curse the arts in {him} from here, across a hundred li

ok.log: Somewhere far off, the water in {npc} stops answering. The Drowning Blade loses a duel a month later to a nobody with a wooden sword. The murim never learns why.

fail.log: The curse slides off, and the effort tears something in you. {npc} feels it, though. {He} knows you are angry, and {he} comes to see why. (-15 health)

choices.text: It is not yours to fix. The murim will deal with {him}

effects.log: It does, eventually, with eleven elders and a great deal of blood. Your arts die with {npc}, which is what you wanted, and the villages blame the lake for the drowning, which you did not.

events.text: {npc} stands on the shore in the rain, the fine sword in {his} hand, and is not ashamed. "You taught me that water does not ask permission," {he} says. "So I stopped asking."

choices.text: Take the arts back: wrap {him} in water and unmake the meridians you opened

ok.log: It is like pulling a river back up a mountain. When it is done {npc} lies in the shallows, an ordinary human, alive, weeping for the first time since {he} was a child.

fail.log: {He} is better than you thought, with your own arts against you. {He} leaves you bleeding in the shallows and walks back up the mountain. (-25 health)

choices.text: Kill {him}. You made this; you end it

effects.log: One coil. One breath. The lake is very quiet afterwards, and you do not eat for a year. You never teach anyone anything for a long time after that.

choices.text: Forgive {him}, and tell {him} what water really does: it gives itself away

effects.log: {npc} laughs at you. Then {he} stops laughing. {He} stands in the rain a long time before {he} goes, and you cannot tell what {he} has decided.

events.text: Years later {npc} comes back, grey at the temples, without the fine sword. {He} carries a bundle of paper: the names of every family {he} drowned, and how {he} has paid each one. "Forty-one," {he} says. "I have found thirty-eight. I wanted you to know I am still counting."

choices.text: Count with {him}. Tell {him} where the last three went

effects.log: The rain has told you everything for six hundred years. Three names, three villages. {npc} walks to all of them. When {he} dies {he} is buried on your shore, and the stone says only: Forty-one.

choices.text: Tell {him} the counting is the penance, not the number

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly, and does not stop counting. Some debts are paid by the paying.

choices.text: Say nothing. Some things you do not get to be forgiven for by a lake

effects.log: {npc} waits until dark, bows to the water, and goes. You hear that {he} spent the rest of {his} life ferrying people across a flood river for free.

events.text: A summer flood comes down the valley and takes a whole hamlet with it. In the brown water of your lake, among the roof thatch and the drowned pigs, a child of eight is clinging to a door. {He} sees your eye open beside {him}, the size of a cartwheel, and does not let go of the door, and does not scream either.

choices.text: Carry {him} to the shore on your head

mem.note: pulled me out of the flood

effects.log: You set {npc} on the rock. {He} stands there dripping and looks at you and says: "Is everyone else dead?" You do not lie to {him}. {He} nods, and sits down, and does not leave.

choices.text: Push the door to the village downriver, where there are humans

effects.log: The door bumps into a fisherman's boat a li downriver. A year later the same child walks back up the valley, alone, and sits on your shore. {He} has come to say thank you, and does not seem to know how to leave.

events.text: {npc} is twelve, lives in a lean-to on your shore, catches fish with {his} hands and talks to you every evening whether you answer or not. Today {he} has made a sword out of a pine branch and asks, very seriously, if you know any sword arts.

choices.text: You know water. Teach {him} water

effects.log: Every morning for years: breathing at dawn, forms on the rock, falls into the lake. You are a terrible teacher at first. By the third year you are a very good one. By the fifth year {npc} is better than anyone in the valley.

choices.text: Send {him} to a proper sect with a scale as a token

effects.log: {npc} cries all the way to the sect gate and gets in on the strength of a serpent scale the elders cannot explain. {He} comes back every winter and practises on the rock, and corrects the sect's forms with yours.

events.text: {npc} is grown, and has gone into the murim, and has come back. {He} crawls the last li to your shore with a poisoned wound across {his} ribs, black at the edges. The poison is a demonic art: it eats qi. Yours could burn it out. It would cost you years.

choices.text: Breathe into the wound

mem.note: burned the poison out with its own life

effects.log: All night, a serpent's breath on a human chest. By morning the black is gone, and so are thirty years of your cultivation. {npc} wakes, sees how still you are, and understands what you paid.

choices.text: Find the antidote herb on the cliff instead

ok.log: Up a cliff no serpent should climb, a purple-flowered herb in a crack. {npc} lives. {He} jokes later that {he} owes {his} life to a snake who can climb.

fail.log: There is no herb. You come back down and breathe into the wound after all, half a night later than you should have. {npc} lives, but walks with a stick for the rest of {his} life.

events.text: It has come. Thunder rolls up the valley the way it has rolled in your dreams for a thousand years, and high in the black cloud something turns over and over and shines: a pearl, falling. On the same night riders with torches come down the valley road. The demonic sect has learned where {npc} sleeps. {He} is standing on the rock with your arts and {his} pine-branch courage, alone, looking up at you. "Go," {he} says. "I know what that is. Go."

choices.text: Stay. Turn your back on the sky and come down to the rock

effects.log: You lower your head from the storm. The riders see what comes up out of the lake to stand beside {npc}, and turn their horses. The pearl falls somewhere into the sea. You never climb again. You teach {npc} everything, and {npc} becomes the greatest sword of the age, and comes back to the lake every spring until {he} is old, and then {his} disciples come, and then theirs.

choices.text: Climb. {He} has your arts; trust them

ok.log: Up into the storm, claws open, the light so close it burns your eyes. It slips past your claw by a finger. When you come down at dawn the shore is scorched, and seven riders lie on it, and {npc} is sitting on the rock, bleeding, grinning. "Next time," {he} says.

fail.log: The storm throws you back into the lake. You come up to find {npc} alive among fallen riders, holding a broken sword, very calm. You chose the sky and lost it, and {he} held the shore anyway. (-20 health)

choices.text: Drown the road first, then climb

ok.log: The valley road becomes a river in a breath, riders and all. Then up into the cloud, late, the pearl already far above. You touch its light and fall back. Some nights you can have half of everything.

fail.log: You flood the road and the storm closes over the pearl while you do it. {npc} is safe. The sky is quiet. You lie in the lake for a long time and do not regret it, mostly. (-15 health)

events.text: {npc} is old now, white-haired, the most famous sword under heaven, and still comes to the lake in spring. {He} sits on the rock where {he} first held a pine branch and says: "When you go up, let me be the one who sees. I have been practising the word for fifty years."

choices.text: Promise {him}

mem.note: promised I would be its witness

effects.log: "Dragon," {npc} says, to practise, and laughs at {him}self. It is the best sound you have heard in a century.

choices.text: Tell {him} not to wait for you. Live

effects.log: "I have lived," {npc} says. "This is what I did with it." {He} comes again the next spring, and the one after.

events.text: Three mountains to the north there is another pool, and in it another serpent: bone-white, older than you by a century, scarred along one flank where something once failed to kill it. When it breathes, your lake tastes of iron. It has four claws too. There is one pearl falling in this part of the sky.
events.arc: The Serpent of the Northern Pool

choices.text: Rise and roar across the mountains so it knows you

effects.log: A roar comes back that knocks the snow off three peaks. The villages between the pools board their windows for a month. So. It knows you.

choices.text: Go and look at it, quietly, through the rain

ok.log: You watch it for a whole night through a curtain of rain. It is hurt more than it lets anyone see. It also, you are almost sure, watched you back.

fail.log: It sees you on the ridge and comes out of its pool like a white landslide. You go home faster than you came. (-10 health)

choices.text: Ignore it. The sky is large

effects.log: You ignore it for years. It ignores you back, loudly, every time it thunders.

events.text: A storm sits over the ridge between your pools. Both of you climb into it at the same moment, and meet in the black cloud halfway up: white coils, green coils, hail like stones. There is no pearl tonight. There is only the other one.
events.arc: The Serpent of the Northern Pool

choices.text: Fight it in the cloud

ok.log: You throw it out of the cloud. It falls three thousand feet into its own pool and the spray puts out a forest fire. In the morning the whole province is talking about it.

fail.log: It wraps you and takes you down through the hail to the ridge and leaves you there, bleeding, in front of a village. It could have killed you. It did not. (-25 health)

choices.text: Give it the storm. There will be other storms

effects.log: You sink out of the cloud. The white serpent climbs alone until dawn and catches nothing. You both know that you let it.

choices.text: Climb past it, higher than either of you has been

ok.log: You leave it below you and climb until the air goes thin and the stars come out above the storm. When you come down, the white serpent is waiting on the ridge, just looking at you.

fail.log: The cloud tears and you fall through it, past the white serpent, which watches you go without moving. (-15 health)

events.text: Hunters have found the northern pool. You hear it in the thunder first, then in the river: iron chains, spears, and the white serpent bellowing, caught. By the time the sun is up they will have its core.
events.arc: The Serpent of the Northern Pool

choices.text: Go, now, through the mountains

ok.log: You come down on the hunters out of the rain. Chains break. The white serpent gets free and fights beside you until the shore is empty. Then the two of you lie in its pool, bleeding into the same water, and say nothing at all. Nothing needs saying.

fail.log: You get it free and take a spear through the coils doing it. It drags you into its pool before the hunters can finish you. You wake in its water, and it is coiled around you, keeping watch. (-25 health)

choices.text: Let the hunters do what you never could

effects.log: It breaks free on its own at dawn, half its scales gone. It never again roars at your pool. It just looks south, toward you, every time it thunders.

choices.text: Call a flood down the hunters' road, from here

ok.log: The hunters' camp goes down the valley in the dark. In the morning the white serpent is free, and a single white scale lies on the rock by your pool. It has been carried three mountains.

fail.log: The flood goes the wrong way. The white serpent gets free alone, wounded, and does not know you tried. (-10 health)

events.text: In a long, slow summer storm the white serpent speaks to you for the first time, in the old way, through thunder. "Two hundred years we have fought for one pearl," it says. "I am tired, and I am still not going to let you have it. Tell me why you want the sky."
events.arc: The Serpent of the Northern Pool

choices.text: Tell it the truth

effects.log: You tell it about the heron, a child at the waterside, the villages you watched grow old. It tells you about its own: a monk, a burned temple, a girl who drowned. When the storm passes, neither of you has given up the pearl. Both of you have stopped hating the other for wanting it.

choices.text: Tell it that is none of its business

effects.log: It laughs, a long rumble that rolls across both valleys. "Good," it says. "I would have been disappointed." Next storm, it fights you harder.

choices.text: Ask it why it wants the sky

ok.log: It is quiet so long you think it has gone. "To see if I was right," it says at last, "to wait." You understand that better than you would like to.

fail.log: It does not answer. The thunder moves on. But it asked, and that has never happened before.

events.text: You are a Cloud-Seeker now, and so is the white serpent. The storms belong to both of you. Tonight a pearl shows itself high in the clouds over the ridge between your pools, and both of you see it in the same flash. It is close. It is meant for one claw.

choices.text: Race it up the storm

ok.log: Your claw closes on light. For a breath you hold it, and the world goes white, and then it slips like wet soap and is gone. The white serpent, a body length below, saw you touch it. It says nothing all the way down.

fail.log: The white serpent is faster. Its claw closes on the pearl, and the pearl slips through it, and it falls past you roaring. Neither of you has it. You almost laugh. (-20 health)

choices.text: Climb together, not against each other

ok.log: It hesitates, then lets you climb beside it. Two coils in one cloud. The pearl outruns you both, but you go higher together than either of you ever has alone.

fail.log: It thinks it is a trick, and lashes you aside. The pearl is lost in the confusion. (-15 health)

choices.text: Hold back and watch where the pearl goes

effects.log: It goes out to sea, and down, into the deep water off the eastern coast. You have learned more from one watching than from ten climbings. The white serpent climbs until dawn and catches nothing.

events.text: The white serpent comes to your lake in daylight, which it has never done. It is old now, even for one of you. It lays its head on your shore beside yours, the way humans sit beside each other at a fire.

choices.text: Lie beside it until dark

effects.log: Neither of you speaks. Fishermen row out from the far shore just to look at two serpents asleep in the sun. One of them paints it. The painting is called Truce.

choices.text: Offer it the next pearl

effects.log: "No," it says, very quietly. "You climb. I climb. We see." It is the closest thing to friendship either of you has ever had.

choices.text: Ask it why it really came

ok.log: "I wanted someone to remember me," it says, "if I fall." You promise. It looks surprised that you mean it.

fail.log: It slides back into the water without answering. But it came. That says enough.

events.text: A hunter clan has put a price on both your cores, and the hunters have learned the trick of fighting one serpent while the other is in the clouds. Tonight they are at the white serpent's pool. The sky above you is perfect for climbing.

choices.text: Leave the sky and go north

effects.log: You arrive with the rain behind you. The hunters scatter. The white serpent looks at you, then at the perfect sky behind you, and understands what you gave up.

choices.text: Climb, and trust it to hold

ok.log: It holds. When you come down, the hunters' banners are floating in its pool. It does not reproach you. It would have done the same.

fail.log: It holds, barely, and loses a claw doing it. When the next storm comes, it does not climb. You climbed. It did not. That is the whole story. (-10 health)

events.text: A grey-bearded hunter with a hooked spear camps on your shore for a month and does nothing but watch. {He} is of the Cheon clan, who have hunted great beasts for nine generations, and on {his} belt hang three teeth you recognise as Imugi teeth. {He} is not looking for your core. {He} is looking for one scale.
events.arc: The Hunters of the Reverse Scale

choices.text: Show {him} the whole of you, every one of the eighty-one scales, and dare {him}

effects.log: {npc} studies you for an hour from the rock, unafraid. Then {he} smiles, a terrible, polite smile, and packs up {his} camp. {He} saw what {he} came for.

choices.text: Stay deep, all month, and let {him} see nothing

effects.log: {npc} leaves with nothing. But you know the Cheon clan. They will send someone younger, with better eyes.

choices.text: Speak to {him}

ok.log: "Nine generations," you say. "How many of you came home?" {npc} is quiet a long time. "Enough," {he} says. But {he} leaves the next morning without {his} spear.

fail.log: {npc} only nods, as if a talking serpent were a thing {he} expected, and writes something down.

events.text: The younger hunter with better eyes comes: a Cheon youth of twenty, sent alone to swim your lake and find the reverse scale, the one scale under the chin that grows the wrong way. {He} dives too deep, too long, and is drowning, a few paces from your throat.
events.arc: The Hunters of the Reverse Scale

choices.text: Save {him}. Lift {him} up into the air

mem.note: saved me, though I came to kill it

effects.log: You carry {npc} up under your chin, which is the only way to carry {him}. {He} coughs up the lake on the shore and looks at you. {He} has seen the reverse scale now. You both know it.

choices.text: Let the lake decide

effects.log: The lake decides. The Cheon clan finds the body on the shore a week later, and the old hunter weeps over it, and swears.

choices.text: Save {him}, and turn your head so {he} never sees the scale

mem.note: saved me, though I came to kill it

ok.log: A coil under {him}, a slow rise, your head turned away the whole time. {npc} comes up into the air with no idea where the scale is, and every idea what you are.

fail.log: You save {npc}, but in the dark water {he} grabs the first thing {he} can reach, and it is the scale that grows the wrong way. The rage almost takes you. You hold it. Just.

events.text: Black iron chains across the river mouth, sunk with stone anchors, hung with hooks. A net of iron big enough to hold a war junk. The Cheon clan has hired a hundred hands and three cultivators. It is not subtle. It does not need to be.
events.arc: The Hunters of the Reverse Scale

choices.text: Break the chains before they finish

ok.log: You take the anchor stones one by one in the night and carry them out to the deep. In the morning the chains hang slack and the hired hands are going home.

fail.log: The hooks bite. You tear free and leave scales in the iron, and the Cheon clan holds them up to the light and smiles. (-20 health)

choices.text: Leave the lake by the underground river and let them guard an empty pool

effects.log: Six months in the dark under the mountain. When you come back, the chains are rusting and the hired hands are gone. The Cheon clan is not.

choices.text: Talk to the hired hands, one by one, at night

effects.log: A voice from the river at night, asking a boatman how many children he has. By the end of the month the Cheon clan cannot hire a single hand on the whole river.

events.text: They come in a storm, which is clever: the storm that calls you up is the storm that hides them. Thirty Cheon hunters on the shore and in boats, spears like a forest, and the old hunter at the front, white-haired now, with a single long needle of cold iron meant for one scale under your chin.
events.arc: The Hunters of the Reverse Scale

choices.text: Fight them on the shore, in the open

ok.log: The needle touches your reverse scale and the rage comes up through you like the sea through a broken dyke. Afterwards the Cheon clan has no hunters left under the age of sixty. The old hunter is alive. You let him be. He has nothing left to hunt.

fail.deathCause: the Cheon clan's needle under your reverse scale
fail.log: The needle goes in under the reverse scale and the rage is not enough. The last thing you see is the old hunter, kneeling by your head, his hand on your scales, saying something that might be an apology. A smith in the south will work your scales for nine years into a blade the murim will kill for.

choices.text: Go down into the abyss and wait them out

effects.log: Down where no spear reaches, under a thousand feet of black water, you wait. Three days, then thirty. The storm passes. The pearl passes. The Cheon clan goes home with nothing, and the old hunter dies that winter.

choices.text: Pull the storm down onto the lake itself

ok.log: The storm comes down out of the sky onto the water like a fist. Boats overturn. Spears float. Nobody dies, which is harder than killing them all, and the Cheon clan understands exactly what you chose.

fail.log: The storm will not come down. You go into the abyss bleeding, with the needle snapped off in your side. (-25 health)

choices.text: Call on the young Cheon you pulled out of the lake

effects.log: The young Cheon you pulled out of the lake steps between the needle and your throat. "It saved me," the youth says, "when it could have let me drown." The hunt breaks on that. Clans are made of families, and families have to sit at one table afterwards.

events.text: Another hunter. They come every few decades now, with spears, nets, bait, poison, prayers. This one has a wanted notice from some magistrate offering a fortune for a flood serpent's core, and the patient eyes of someone who has done this before.

choices.text: Frighten them off with a wall of water

effects.log: A wave up the beach to the treeline. The hunter goes home and tells everyone the lake is not worth it. Some of them listen.

choices.text: Lead them on a chase down the river until they are lost

ok.log: Three weeks of glimpses, wakes, false trails. The hunter ends up two provinces away, convinced you are a different serpent entirely.

fail.log: The hunter is better than you thought and gets one spear into you before you lose them. (-12 health)

choices.text: Fight

ok.log: It is over before the hunter understands it has begun. You leave the spear on the shore, broken, as a message.

fail.log: Poison on the spearhead. You win, but you are sick for a decade. (-20 health)

events.text: An old swordsmith comes to the shore with no weapon and no bait. "I have made swords for forty years," {he} says, "and they all break eventually. I want to make one that does not. I am not asking for your life. I am asking for one scale, if you have one to spare."
events.arc: The Smith Who Asked for a Scale

choices.text: Give {him} a shed scale

mem.note: gave me a scale for the sword

effects.log: {npc} wraps the scale in silk, bows nine times, and walks home. {He} spends the rest of {his} life on one sword.

choices.text: Give {him} nothing: a sword of you will make others want more of you

effects.log: {npc} nods. "You are right," {he} says, "and I would have done it anyway." {He} leaves, and the shore is quiet.

choices.text: Tear one from your own flank and give {him} a living scale

mem.note: tore out its own scale for me

effects.log: Blood in the water. {npc} stares at the scale, still warm, still faintly green-lit, and cannot speak. (-10 health)

events.text: {npc} comes back, much older, carrying a sword wrapped in oilcloth. {He} unwraps it on the shore: grey-green, rippled like water, humming faintly when the wind moves over it. "It is finished," {he} says. "I came to ask what I should do with it."
events.arc: The Smith Who Asked for a Scale

choices.text: Throw it into the lake. A thing like that should belong to no one

effects.log: {npc} throws it without hesitating. It sinks without a splash. For a thousand years swordsmen dive for it, and never find it, and get very good at diving.

choices.text: Give it to whoever guards this valley

effects.log: The sword goes to a young wandering swordsman who protects the valley for years. It is called the Lake Scale, and nobody ever learns where the scale came from.

choices.text: Let {him} keep it: {he} earned it

effects.log: {npc} hangs it over {his} cold forge and dies with it there. The murim fights over it for three generations. Some of what you give away does not stay given.

events.text: Two elders of the Murim Alliance come to your shore in a covered boat: one from a sword sect, one a Buddhist monk with a strand of beads. They have been sent to decide whether you are a monster, to be hunted, or a guardian, to be left in peace. They are clearly not in agreement about which.

choices.text: Rise and speak to them, plainly

ok.log: You talk for an afternoon about floods and rain and the people on your shore. The monk smiles. The swordsman takes notes and looks uneasy, which is also a good sign.

fail.log: Your voice cracks a boat plank. The swordsman draws. The monk stops him with one hand. It is not the meeting you hoped for.

choices.text: Show them the village shrines on your shore and say nothing

effects.log: They walk the shore for a day. Rice cakes, carvings, a little stone with a fisherman's name on it. They row away having said almost nothing to each other.

choices.text: Stay down. You do not owe them an audience

effects.log: They wait three days, then leave. The report they write has a great deal of guessing in it.

events.text: The Alliance hall is a thousand li away, and you can feel the argument from here: hunters with bounty notices, the valley headmen with petitions, a sword sect whose elder lost a nephew in your lake two hundred years ago. The vote is at the autumn assembly.

choices.text: Send a soft rain over the whole assembly, and nowhere else

effects.log: Every elder in the hall walks home damp and thoughtful. It is very hard to vote against something that can do that politely.

choices.text: Send a storm, to remind them what you are

effects.log: The hall roof comes off in the second hour. The vote is moved indoors somewhere else, and is not friendly.

choices.text: Send nothing. Let your centuries speak

effects.log: You do nothing, and wait, and find you are as nervous as any human waiting on a verdict.

events.text: A rider comes up the valley road, an Alliance messenger, and reads the verdict aloud to the water, voice shaking. Everything you have done for four hundred years sits on the scales of a hall full of strangers.

choices.text: Listen

ok.log: "The great serpent of the lake is a guardian of the people, and any who hunt it hunt against the Alliance." The rider looks up from the scroll, very relieved. So, you find, are you.

fail.log: "The great serpent of the lake is a calamity beast, and a bounty is set upon its core." The rider rides away very fast. You lie in the deep and think about humans for a long time.

choices.text: Rise before the rider can read it and tell {npc} to go home: it is not theirs to decide

effects.log: The scroll goes back unread. The Alliance never publishes the verdict, and both sides claim it went their way.

events.text: Because the Alliance has named you a guardian, the Alliance now asks things of you. A demonic cult fleet is coming up the great river toward the valley towns, and the Alliance would be grateful, the letter says, very carefully, if the river could perhaps be unfriendly.

choices.text: Be unfriendly

ok.log: Forty ships go up the river. Six come back down. The Alliance has a festival in your name, which you do not attend.

fail.log: The cult has a sorcerer with a hook of black iron, and it costs you. The fleet still turns back. (-20 health)

choices.text: Refuse: a guardian is not a weapon

effects.log: The Alliance is offended, then thoughtful. They fight the fleet themselves. It costs them, and they remember whose river it was they fought on.

events.text: The bounty has done its work. Every few years another band of hopefuls camps on your shore with a copy of the Alliance notice. And now, today, a little girl from the valley has walked all the way to the Alliance hall with a petition signed by nine villages, asking them to take it back.

choices.text: Go and stand behind the villages, so the Alliance can see you

ok.log: The Alliance looks out of its window at a serpent the size of a hill, lying quietly in a field of signatures. The bounty is withdrawn the same afternoon.

fail.log: The Alliance sees a monster at its gate and nothing else. The girl walks home with her petition. You carry her, and that is the part of the story the valley keeps.

choices.text: Stay away: if you go, they will only see a monster

effects.log: The petition is read aloud in the assembly hall. It is not enough, yet. But it is read, and next decade it is read again, louder.

events.text: You are a Cloud-Seeker. Your body knows it before you do: when the first thunder comes over the ridge, your coils are already rising. This is the first storm you have ever climbed on purpose. Above the cloud there is only cold and light, and somewhere, maybe, the pearl.

choices.text: Climb as high as you can

ok.log: Up through hail and dark until the cloud thins and you burst into moonlight above a sea of storm. Nothing up here but stars. You hang there a long time before you fall back down.

fail.log: Lightning finds you halfway up. You fall into the lake so hard the villages think a mountain has dropped into it. (-20 health)

choices.text: Climb slowly, learning the storm's shape

effects.log: You learn that every storm has a spine, a column of wind that carries what rides it. Next time you will find it faster.

choices.text: Stay in the lake and watch it this once

effects.log: You watch the lightning from the water, and the villagers watch you watching it. They will talk about it all winter: the night the serpent looked up.

events.text: The great storm of the century: three days of thunder, the river over its banks, a typhoon coming in off the sea. If there is ever a storm to reach the pearl in, it is this one. If there is ever a storm to die in, it is also this one.

choices.text: Climb into the heart of it

ok.log: Inside the eye of the typhoon there is a silence like a temple. And there, turning slowly, it is: the pearl. You reach. It turns away like a shy thing. But you have seen it close, and it has seen you.

fail.deathCause: the great typhoon, reaching for the pearl
fail.log: The storm tears you from the sky and throws you onto the mountain. You lie on the rocks a month before you can crawl back to water. (-35 health)

choices.text: Ride the edge of it, where the wind is kind

ok.log: You ride the outer arm of the storm like a fisherman rides a current. You do not see the pearl. You see how high you will need to go.

fail.log: The edge is not as kind as it looked. You come down in a rice paddy two valleys over and have to explain yourself to a very surprised farmer. (-10 health)

choices.text: Use the storm's strength to hold back the river for the villages

effects.log: Three days holding a river in your coils while the pearl flashes once, somewhere far above, and goes. The villages stand on their roofs and see a serpent wrapped around their river like a dyke.

events.text: You have climbed storm after storm now. The villagers have a word for the sound you make going up, like a bell being pulled through water. Children run outside when they hear it. Some of them run toward the lake.

choices.text: Take one of the children's faces up with you in your mind

effects.log: There is a girl with a red ribbon who always waves. You climb for her, this time, and get higher than you ever have.

choices.text: Climb for yourself

effects.log: Some climbs are only yours. The sky does not care why you come. That is almost a comfort.

choices.text: Warn the children back with a single roll of thunder

effects.log: They scatter home, giggling and terrified. A storm with a serpent in it is no place for children. They will be grown before they understand you were protecting them.

events.text: Thunder over the ridge again. The old ache in your claws.

choices.text: Climb

ok.log: Up, and up, and nothing. But higher than last time.

fail.log: The storm throws you back down. You will be here when the next one comes. (-12 health)

choices.text: Let this one pass

effects.log: Not every storm is yours. Sitting one out is also a kind of climbing.

events.text: You see it for the first time with your own eyes. Not in a dream: real. A point of light falling out of a thunderhead over the eastern sea, turning over and over, the colour of moonlight in milk. It is so far away that a human would take it for a shooting star. You know exactly what it is.

choices.text: Follow it to where it falls

ok.log: You follow it a hundred li to the coast and see it strike the sea in a column of steam. It is gone by the time you reach the water, but now you know: they fall where the storms are worst, over the deepest water.

fail.log: You lose it in the cloud. Crossing the coastal hills at night, a farmer with a pitchfork does his best. (-10 health)

choices.text: Watch it all the way down, and remember everything

effects.log: You watch it fall, very slowly, the way a leaf falls. You memorise the storm, the wind, the hour. When it is gone your whole body aches as if something has been taken from it.

events.text: An old fisherman on the coast tells you, through his nets, that he saw it too. "A falling star that stopped falling," he says. "It hung over the water for the length of a prayer. Then it went down. My grandmother said that is a pearl looking for a dragon. Are you a dragon?"

choices.text: Say yes

effects.log: He nods, satisfied, and goes home and tells everyone a dragon came to his nets. By spring the coast is full of shrines to a dragon that has not happened yet.

choices.text: Say not yet

effects.log: "Not yet," he says, tasting it. "Good. I am not yet either. Not yet a rich man, not yet a dead one." He laughs, and you find you are laughing too.

choices.text: Ask him to watch for the next one, and tell you

effects.log: He watches until he dies, and his son after him. The coast becomes the only village in the world with a pearl-watch.

events.text: A runner comes to your lake from the coast: a young woman with sea-salt on her sandals, the granddaughter of the old fisherman's son. "Grandfather said to tell you," she gasps. "The pearl-watch saw it. Tonight. Over the black water south of the islands."

choices.text: Go at once

ok.log: You reach the sea at midnight, climb into the storm, and for one heartbeat it is in your claw, cold and alive. It slips. But you know now that it will fit.

fail.log: You are an hour late. Steam is still rising off the black water. (-15 health)

choices.text: Thank her, and send her home with a blessing on the watch

effects.log: The next storm season the village catches more fish than it has in a hundred years. The watch is kept for four more generations, out of gratitude now, not orders.

events.text: The dream comes back, the one you have had since you were a finger long: a shining bead turning over and over in the sky. But now it is closer. Now the bead is not falling. It is coming back, slowly, toward your open claw, and in its light you can see the faces of everyone who ever left you a rice cake.

choices.text: Close the claw in the dream

effects.log: Your claw closes on nothing, and you wake with your foot clenched so hard the scales creak. Close. Closer than ever.

choices.text: Look at the faces instead

effects.log: The heron. A child at the waterside. A fisherman. A swordsman on a rock. You realise you have been carrying them up every storm, and that they are the weight that makes you climb.

events.text: The dream again, and this time a voice in it, neither old nor young: "Who will see you rise?" You wake. There is a village on your shore. You have watched it for six hundred years. You do not know the name of a single child in it.

choices.text: Learn their names

effects.log: It takes a winter of listening from the reeds. By spring you know every name in the village and which children are afraid of the water. You start with them.

choices.text: The sky does not need witnesses. It needs strength

effects.log: You go back to sleep. The dream does not come back for a long time, and when it does, the voice is quieter.

events.text: A village two valleys away has walked to your shore with its whole population: forty families, three oxen, a headman with a bowl. Their well has gone dry. Their children are drinking mud. They have heard that the four-clawed serpent can bless a place.

choices.text: Go with them and bless the well

effects.log: You put your head down the dry well and breathe. Water rises from the dark, cold and sweet. The village renames itself Serpent Well, and never runs dry again.

choices.text: Teach their headman where water hides under the ground

effects.log: Three days of lessons in a voice like distant thunder. The headman digs where you said. The village becomes famous for its well-diggers, who never say who taught them.

choices.text: Ask a tribute first

effects.log: An ox, every year, forever. They agree without arguing. Their well fills. Their grandchildren will still be leading oxen to your shore, and hating it a little.

events.text: Heaven has noticed. A cold voice in the thunder, the kind that does not need to raise itself: the blessing of wells is not a serpent's right. The Jade Court's clerks keep accounts, and yours are in the red.

choices.text: Accept the punishment: lightning, once

effects.log: It strikes you on the shore in front of the village. They see you take it and not move. The story goes everywhere: the serpent that was punished for their water. (-25 health)

choices.text: Argue with heaven

ok.log: You argue for three days in thunder. Heaven, it turns out, has rules about water and no rules about thirst. The account is closed. The clerks are annoyed.

fail.log: Heaven does not argue. Heaven strikes, twice. (-30 health)

choices.text: Hide in the abyss until heaven forgets

effects.log: Heaven does not forget. It does get busy, which is nearly as good.

events.text: A famine year. The valley magistrate has filled the government granary to the roof and sold none of it, waiting for prices to rise. A farmer's widow comes to your shore with her last child on her back and asks you, very simply, to curse him.

choices.text: Curse him: every grain he hoards turns to river sand

ok.log: In the morning the magistrate opens his granary and sand pours out, and only sand, until his men open the free sacks for the valley. Those come out rice. The magistrate takes the hint.

fail.log: The curse slides off the seals and talismans on the granary door. The magistrate has been ready for something like you. Not for long.

choices.text: Flood the granary wall and let the valley take what floats

effects.log: A night of rain, a wall that gives way, a river of rice sacks floating down the valley road. Nobody starves that winter. The magistrate writes to the capital.

choices.text: Curse no one. Send the widow fish instead, every day until spring

effects.log: Every morning there are fish on the widow's doorstep, and her neighbours', and theirs. The magistrate sells his rice at a loss in the spring and never understands why nobody needed it.

events.text: The magistrate's letter has reached the capital. A court exorcist arrives with a cart of talismans, a sealing bell, and a decree naming you a rebel beast. The valley has hidden you nothing, because you are a lake. But they line the road to watch the exorcist pass, and nobody sells him food.

choices.text: Meet the exorcist at the shore and let the valley see

ok.log: The exorcist looks at the valley, at you, at the decree. Then he folds the decree and goes back to the capital with a report about a magistrate instead.

fail.log: The sealing bell rings, and something in you goes numb for a year. The valley gets you through it with offerings, the way you got them through the famine. (-20 health)

choices.text: Shatter the bell with thunder before he rings it

effects.log: Bronze shards rain over the shore. The exorcist goes home deaf in one ear and the court sends hunters instead of exorcists, which is a kind of promotion.

events.text: River pirates: a dozen long boats with ragged sails and a chief who has heard all the stories about the lake and does not believe one. They come for the fishing villages on your shore at night, with torches.
events.arc: The Pirates of the Great River

choices.text: Rise in the middle of the fleet

ok.log: The chief believes the stories now, briefly, from the bottom of the lake. The rest of the fleet goes home and starts a new life as honest ferrymen.

fail.log: Fire arrows and a great harpoon crossbow bought somewhere in the south. The pirates break in the end, but you pay for every one. (-18 health)

choices.text: Fog the lake so thick they row in circles until dawn

effects.log: All night, oars and curses in the mist. At dawn the fleet is in the middle of the lake, exhausted, surrounded by every fishing boat on the shore with a net and a grudge.

choices.text: Let the villages defend themselves, this once

effects.log: They do, mostly. Two houses burn. The villages learn they can fight, and also that the lake does not always come.

events.text: A boy who was six when the pirates came is the new village headman. He comes to the shore with a carved tablet that says, in his own clumsy hand, Guardian of the Shore, and asks permission to hang it.
events.arc: The Pirates of the Great River

choices.text: Allow it

effects.log: It hangs on the jetty for two hundred years, re-carved every generation, always in a slightly clumsy hand, out of tradition.

choices.text: Ask him to carve the names of the village dead instead

effects.log: He carves the names. Then, underneath, smaller, he carves Guardian of the Shore anyway. Some arguments you do not win.

events.text: A very old monk asks permission to count your scales. "Eighty-one," he says, "is the number for a dragon. Nine by nine. I would like to know before I die whether you have them all."

choices.text: Lie still and let him count

effects.log: He counts for six days, very slowly, one bead per scale. Eighty-one. He sits back, satisfied. "And one more," he says, "under the chin, the wrong way. Do not let anyone touch that one."

choices.text: Ask him what happens if one is missing

effects.log: "Then you are a serpent who has had a hard life," he says, "which is also a thing heaven respects." You think about that for a long time.

events.text: The monk's disciple comes, then the disciple's disciple. The temple on the hill has a tradition now: once in a lifetime, a monk counts the serpent's scales. This one is a nervous young nun who keeps losing her place.

choices.text: Help her count by flexing each scale in turn

effects.log: Each scale lifts and shines like a coin as she reaches it. She laughs out loud, then covers her mouth. Eighty-one. She will be abbess one day, and she will tell this story to every novice.

choices.text: Show her the reverse scale, and trust her

effects.log: She looks at it a long time and does not touch it. "Thank you," she says. "I will not write this one down." She never does.

events.text: The valley shaman is holding a gut for you: drums, bells, a table of rice cakes and fruit and a whole pig, and she dances on the shore all night in a robe of five colours. She is very good. Halfway through, her eyes roll up and she speaks with your voice. Or what she thinks is your voice.

choices.text: Rise and speak with your real one, gently

effects.log: The drums stop dead. The shaman, very calm for someone who has just met her god, nods and says: "Close enough." The valley talks about it for a hundred years.

choices.text: Let her speak for you; she says kinder things than you would

effects.log: Through her, you promise good harvests and safe childbirth and forgive a boy for a stone thrown long ago. You decide afterwards to keep all of the promises.

choices.text: Eat the pig

effects.log: One head out of the water and the pig is gone. The shaman does not miss a beat. "The lord is pleased," she cries, and the drums go wild.

events.text: The shaman's granddaughter holds the rite now, and she has added something: a paper dragon with four claws, burned at dawn so the smoke can rise to the sky in your place. "Practice," she says to the water, a little shy. "For when you go."

choices.text: Rise into the smoke, so the valley sees

effects.log: A serpent's head in the smoke of a burning paper dragon, at dawn. Every child there will be able to describe it to their grandchildren.

choices.text: Ask her to keep doing it after you are gone, too

effects.log: She promises. In the valley, centuries later, they still burn a paper dragon every spring, and only the old people remember why.

events.text: A wandering painter has come to the lake to paint you, and has been there a month without a single brushstroke. {He} says {he} cannot find your eyes. Every painter who has painted a dragon has failed at the eyes.

choices.text: Look at {him}, for a whole afternoon

effects.log: {npc} paints in a fever, all night, and does not dot the eyes. "If I dot them," {he} says, "it will fly away." It is the most famous painting in the province for three hundred years.

choices.text: Close your eyes

effects.log: {npc} paints you sleeping. It is very peaceful, and people buy copies to hang over sickbeds. {He} is a little disappointed and very rich.

choices.text: Splash {him} and {his} silk for impertinence

effects.log: The ink runs into a shape like a storm with something in it. {npc} keeps it. It is the best thing {he} ever did, and {he} did not do it.

events.text: Word comes that {npc}'s painting of you has been bought by a hunter clan, who are studying it for weak spots. {npc}, old now, has rowed out onto the lake alone, ashamed, to tell you.

choices.text: Forgive {him}

effects.log: "A painting is not a serpent," you tell {him}. "They will learn that." {npc} goes home lighter, and paints only landscapes after that, every one with a lake in it.

choices.text: Ask {him} to paint a second one, wrong on purpose

effects.log: A beautiful painting with eighty scales and the reverse scale on the wrong side. It sells for twice as much. Two hunter clans buy copies. You are delighted.

events.text: There is a ferry across your lake, run by the same family for six generations. Each ferry-keeper, on the day they inherit the pole, pours a cup of rice liquor into the water halfway across. The new one is fourteen and so frightened that most of the cup goes on the boat.

choices.text: Rise and take the cup from the air before it spills

effects.log: A head the size of the ferry, a tongue, a cup of rice liquor, gone. The fourteen-year-old screams, then laughs, and poles for years without fear of anything.

choices.text: Swim under the ferry the whole way, steadying it

effects.log: The calmest crossing in the history of the ferry. The passengers say the lake was like a floor. The new ferry-keeper knows better, and pours a second cup on the way back.

events.text: A storm on the lake, the ferry caught halfway, nine passengers and a bride's family dowry chest. The ferry-keeper who spilled the cup is old now and shouting into the wind, not for help. For you.

choices.text: Carry the ferry to shore on your back

effects.log: Nine passengers, a bride's chest and an old ferry-keeper ride a serpent across a storm. The wedding goes ahead. The bride insists on bowing to the lake before she bows to her husband's parents.

choices.text: Hold the storm off the boat with your coils

ok.log: A ring of calm water around one small boat in a raging lake. They row the rest of the way themselves, which they will be proud of for the rest of their lives.

fail.log: The waves get past you and the dowry chest goes overboard. Everyone lives. The chest is found on the shore a month later, coiled in seaweed, which the bride takes as a blessing. (-15 health)

events.text: You shed. The old skin, translucent and enormous, catches on the pines up the hillside and hangs there like a silver banner a li long. By noon three sects have sent disciples to claim it. A flood serpent's shed skin makes armour that turns a sword.
events.arc: The Silver Skin on the Hill

choices.text: Give it to the valley villages to cut and sell

effects.log: The villages sell it piece by piece to the sects and are rich for a generation. The sects grumble and pay. For once the people who live next to a monster profit from it.

choices.text: Let the sects fight over it

effects.log: Three days of duels on the hillside over your old skin. You watch from the lake. It is the most entertaining thing that has happened in a century.

choices.text: Burn it with lightning before anyone gets it

effects.log: A whole hillside of silver burns blue for an hour. Nobody wears your skin. The sects remember who decides what is yours.

events.text: A disciple of one of the sects comes back alone, twenty years later, in armour cut from your skin. {He} has worn it through eleven fights and lived through all of them. {He} wants to know if {he} should give it back.
events.arc: The Silver Skin on the Hill

choices.text: Keep it. Wear it well

effects.log: {npc} wears it for another forty years and becomes a byword for the person who cannot be cut down. {He} always says why.

choices.text: Give it to someone who needs it more

effects.log: {npc} thinks about it, and gives it to a girl from the valley going off to join a sect with nothing. The armour has a long, good life.

events.text: An envoy from the royal court arrives under ceremonial parasols with a decree on yellow silk. The king, it says, has heard of a four-clawed serpent in a provincial lake, and graciously grants it a title, a shrine, and the duty of bringing rain to the capital for the length of his reign.

choices.text: Accept the title, and the duty

effects.log: The Lord of the Abyssal Lake, Third Rank. The rain falls on the capital that summer and the king is very pleased with himself. You find the title faintly ridiculous, and keep it.

choices.text: Refuse: rain is not a duty, it is a gift

effects.log: The envoy goes pale. Nobody refuses a king. But a lake is hard to punish, and the court quietly files the decree under Matters Not Pursued.

choices.text: Ask the court for something in return: no more hunters on this lake

ok.log: The envoy writes it into the decree in his own hand. Royal soldiers post notices on every road. The hunters still come, but now they come as criminals.

fail.log: The envoy cannot negotiate for a king and says so, at length. The decree goes back to the capital unsigned by anyone with claws.

events.text: The king who gave you a title is dead. His son, a hard young man, sends a new envoy: the title stands, but the throne requires a scale from the Lord of the Abyssal Lake, to be set into the new royal sword.

choices.text: Send one, freely

effects.log: A scale in a box of black lacquer. The royal sword is the finest in the kingdom, and every king after uses it, and none of them dare make war on a lake. (-8 health)

choices.text: Send a shed scale, dead and grey, with a polite letter

effects.log: The new king understands the message perfectly. He sends you nothing else for the whole of his reign, which suits you.

choices.text: Return the title

effects.log: The title comes back to the capital in an envoy's trembling hands. The young king rages for a week, then forgets. Titles are for humans.

events.text: A child of six has started climbing the hill above your lake every storm, to watch you climb. {His} grandmother drags {him} home by the ear every time, scolding all the way down: "That is a snake, a great big snake, and snakes eat children." The child shouts back up the hill at you, every time: "Dragon!"

choices.text: Climb a little lower on stormy nights, where {he} can see

mem.note: climbed where I could see it

effects.log: Every storm, the same small figure on the hill, shouting the same word. You begin to climb toward it, a little, as well as toward the sky.

choices.text: Visit the grandmother instead, and change her mind

ok.log: You bring the grandmother a carp the size of a child, and lay it on the doorstep, and wait. The next storm the old woman climbs the hill too, grumbling, and does not drag anyone home.

fail.log: The grandmother screams, bars the door, and tells the whole village the snake came for the child. {npc} still climbs the hill. Now {he} goes alone, in secret, which is worse.

choices.text: Stay far away. A child should not be part of this

effects.log: You climb on the far side of the mountain. The child stops coming eventually. Some years later you find you miss the shouting.

events.text: {npc} is grown, and still climbs the hill in storms. {He} has taught {his} own children the word. In the village they call {him} the Dragon-Caller, and laugh, a little. {He} does not mind. "I am only early," {he} says.

choices.text: Tell {him} that when the day comes, {he} must be the first to see

mem.note: asked me to be the first to see

effects.log: {npc} nods as if {he} has been waiting {his} whole life to be asked. {He} has.

choices.text: Come down from the storm, just once, and touch your nose to {his} hand

mem.note: came down out of the storm to me

effects.log: The whole village sees it. Nobody laughs at the Dragon-Caller again.

events.text: On the bottom of the lake there is a layer of everything humans have ever given you: rice bowls, coins, carved tablets, a child's wooden sword, a hunter's broken spear, a bride's hairpin. You lie among them and try to remember who gave each one. You are twelve hundred years old. You remember about half.

choices.text: Try to remember them all

effects.log: It takes a winter. You get to two thirds. The ones you cannot remember you name yourself, so that somebody does.

choices.text: Carry the best of them up to the shore, where the living can see them

effects.log: One morning the villagers find their great-grandparents' offerings laid in a row on the shore, cleaned. They do not know what it means. They put them in the shrine, and some of them cry.

choices.text: Leave them. The sky is up, not down

effects.log: You turn your head toward the light. There will be time to remember when you are a dragon, or when you are not.
